newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels deny asking ransom for hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels deny asking ransom for hostages.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence put a sign up to a window on Thursday denying government claims they were asking for ransom money for their captives.
"Do not lie Mr. Fujimori. Money does not interest us. The demand is freedom of our prisoners," the sign said.

President Alberto Fujimori's government had urged that Japanese companies with representatives held captive not give in to what he called the rebels' "blackmail." Although the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) has in the past kidnapped businessmen and politicians to raise money, there was no evidence this was their aim in the 23-day siege.

Their principal demand since they burst into an exclusive cocktail party and seized the residence on Dec. 17, taking more than 500 guests hostage, has been the release of about 400 jailed comrades. Most of the hostages were later released.

Fujimori, who has vowed not to release the jailed rebels, said he was waiting for "favorable conditions" to send his chief negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, to meet with the rebels in answer to their "open-door" invitation more than a week ago.

Talks stopped abruptly after a first face-to-face meeting 12 days ago between Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini inside the mined and booby-trapped ambassador's residence. Fujimori blamed the stalled negotiations on an impromptu news conference by the guerrillas on New Year's Eve that derailed concessions the two sides had hammered out.

The MRTA responded to Palermo's visit to the residence by freeing 20 captives but they have warned there will be no more releases until the negotiator returns. A steady trickle of releases dried up on Jan. 1 with the rebels still holding top government and security force officials, Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the brother of Fujimori.

In an interview with the CNN television network on Wednesday, the president reiterated a promise he made early in the siege to accept a "commission of guarantors" to oversee a peaceful solution to the crisis.
Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, whose visits inside the compound helped win the release of hostages, has returned to his hometown of Ayacucho in the Andean highlands.
But while Fujimori publicly maintained his tough line against the guerrillas, lambasting them as "terrorists," there was evidence of behind-the-scenes negotiations.

Fujimori said Palermo had been in contact with Cartolini by radio during earlier stages of the crisis and a local newspaper said key presidential adviser Vladimiro Montesinos -- believed by many to be the country's top power-broker -- had met with imprisoned MRTA leader Victor Polay.
Fujimori soothed fears a false move could trigger a violent end to the standoff when he said in a Lima shantytown on Wednesday there would be "no acts of blood" in the siege.

The president's propaganda battle was helped by the publication of photographs in the country's leading weekly news magazine, Caretas, of child guerrillas being trained in the jungle. While denied by the MRTA, police sources have accused the guerrillas of coercing children into their ranks.

In Lima, local and foreign journalists called for the immediate release of a reporter and a translator from Japan's TV Asahi arrested on Tuesday after sneaking past police for a two-hour meeting with the MRTA inside the diplomatic mansion.
"We are waiting for the government to explain on what legal basis they are being held," said Sally Bowen, president of Peru's Foreign Press Association.
